scenes.texte: What would your life be like during the Middle Ages?
Level one. You're a peasant, like nearly nine people out of ten.
You're born in a one-room house with a dirt floor. In winter, the animals sleep inside with you, for the warmth.
At six, you're already working. Scaring birds off the fields, gathering wood, watching the pigs.
The land isn't yours. You owe the lord days of work every week, and the church a tenth of your harvest.
In your early twenties, you marry a girl from the next village. Your parents chose her.
Together, you have seven children. Two of them die before their fifth birthday.
Then comes the summer of 1315. It rains for months, and the wheat rots in the fields.
For two years, there's barely anything to eat. People eat their seed grain, then their animals.
You survive. Your youngest doesn't.
One winter, your wife dies giving birth to your eighth child. She was thirty-two.
Then one morning, you wake up sick. The village healer has nothing for you but herbs, prayers, and a blade to bleed you.
You die at forty-one, in the same room you were born in.
Level two. This time, you're born in town, the son of a shoemaker.
At twelve, your father sends you away. Seven years as an apprentice, in another master's house.
You sleep under the workbench. You're fed, but rarely paid. One mistake, and you're beaten.
The town around you stinks. Waste runs down the middle of the street, and pigs wander everywhere.
At twenty-five, you finally become a master and open your own shop.
Then in 1348, ships bring a new disease from the east. People call it the great mortality.
Your neighbors die within days. Swellings, fever, and then nothing.
In a few years, at least a third of Europe is gone. You lose your wife and two of your sons.
Level three. You're born a lord's son. At seven, you leave home to serve another lord as a page.
At fourteen, you become a squire. You polish armor, care for the horses, and follow your knight into battle.
At twenty-one, you're knighted. A tap of the sword on your shoulder, and your life belongs to war.
In battle, you wear over twenty kilos of steel. You can hardly see, and you can barely breathe.
But it isn't the arrows that kill your friends. On campaign, disease often kills more men than swords.
You come home scarred, rich, and alone. Of the twelve squires you trained with, four are still alive.
Level four. You're the king's eldest son. Your father dies of a fever, and you're crowned at fourteen.
Too young to rule, so your uncles rule for you. And every one of them wants your throne.
You eat nothing until someone else has tasted it first. You trust no one.
At thirty, your barons rebel. You win the war, but your treasury is empty.
And at forty-three, you fall from your horse while hunting. Three days later, you're dead.
Four lives. Four hard lives. So was the Middle Ages really that miserable?
Not quite. The famous life expectancy of thirty is an average, dragged down by all the children who died young.
Make it past childhood, and you could easily reach your fifties or sixties.
And no, people weren't all filthy. Towns had public bathhouses, and people washed far more than we think.

appli.titre: Was life in the Middle Ages really so miserable?
appli.description: Short lives, dirty bodies, empty stomachs: the archives and the skeletons tell another story.

lecon.sousTitre: Hard, yes. But not what you've been told.
